ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
New Commission to look into Centre-State relations 
*401. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Government have proposed to set up a new 
Commission to look into the Centre-State relations; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) the draft terms of reference of the Commission; and 
(d) whether the States have been consulted in the matter? 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIV RAJ V. PATH): 
(a) Yes, Sir. The Government has decided to set up a new Commission to look 
into the Centre-State relations. 
(b) and (c) In terms of its commitment made in the Common Minimum 
Programme, the Government has decided to set up a new Commission to look 
into the issues of Centre-State relations keeping in view the sea-changes that 
have taken place in the polity and ec onomy of India since the Sarkaria 
Commission last looked at these issues over two decades ago. Pursuant to this 
decision, the Government had constituted a Group of Ministers (GOM) for 
finalizing the Terms of Reference (TOR) of the Commission. As per the TOR 
since finalised by the GOM, the Commission would examine and review the 
working of the existing arrangements between the Union and States as per the 
Constitution of India and various 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
pronouncements of the Courts in this regard; address the growing challenges of 
ensuring good governance for promoting welfare of the people, strengthening the unity 
and integrity of the country. Besides, the Commission will also make recommendations 
on the role, responsibility and jurisdiction of Centre vis-a-vis States during major and 
prolonged outbreaks of communal violence, caste violence or any other social conflict 
leading to prolonged and escalated violence; planning and implementation of mega projects; 
effective devolution of powers and autonomy to various local bodies; practice of 
independent planning and budgeting at district leveljinking central assistance with the 
performance of States; positive discrimination in favour of backward states; fiscal 
relations between centre and states; levying duties on goods and services in the 
emerging tax regime; freeing inter-state trade to establish a unified and integrated 
domestic market; setting up a Central Law Enforcement Agency; supporting 
legislation under Article 355, etc. 
(d) No, Sir. 
SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: Sir, it is a fact that many recommendations of the 
Sarkaria Commission, particularly relating to the delegation of powers to the States, 
have not been implemented so far. Therefore will the hon. Minister assure the House 
that such recommendations of the Sarkaria Commission will be implemented without 
waiting for the Report of the new Commission? 
SHRI SHIV RAJ V. PMIL: Sir, majority of the recommendations of the Sarkaria 
Commission have been implemented. The Sarkaria Commission had given 247 
recommendations. Out of 247 recommendations, 179 recommendations have been 
implemented. The Government has not accepted 63 recommendations, and five 
recommendations are pending with the Government. We are discussing the 
recommendations with the State Government to find out as to how they can be 
implemented. 
SHRI T.T.V DHINAKARAN: Sir, it is surprising that the states have not been 
consulted on this matter. The Group of Ministers has already finalised the Terms of 
Reference of the new Commission without ascertaining the views of the States. I 
want to know whether the Government has any proposals to consult the States before 
referring the matterto the new Commission; and if so, when the consultation is likely to 
be made? 
2 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
SHRI SHIV RAJ V. PATIL: Sir, matters of this nature are decided at the 
national level. We have a mechanism of consulting the Chief Ministers also. 
Inter-State Council is the forum where th e Chief Ministers are consulted, and 
this issue, formally or informally, has been discussed with them. Moreover, once 
the commission is appointed, any Government, anybody or any person can put 
its or his views before the Commission for its discussion, and the Terms of 
Reference are omnibus. So, you can include anything you want to include in the 
representation which you will make to this Commission for consideration. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, the hon. Minister has given quite a long list 
of the Terms of Reference according to  which various issues are going to be 
examined by the new Commission which the Government is proposing to set 
up. Some of the issues e.g. linking Central assistance with the performance of 
States, fiscal relations between Centre and States and setting up a Central Law 
Enforcement Agency, as stated by the hon. Minister in the end of paragraph, had 
already been at length deliberated by the States in the Inter-State Council. They 
were earlier resolved. The question of transfer of Centrally sponsored schemes 
particularly, which pertain to the State List, should be transferred to the States 
along with the funds. These were issues which were decided by the National 
Development Council. How is the Government proposing to set up a new 
Commission with all this agenda, without having implemented all those issues 
which were settled earlier? It is very strange! 
MR CHAIRMAN: But it has not been implemented till now. 
SHRI SHIV RAJ V. PATIL: Sir, we have to understand what is the role of 
the National Development Council and how do we look at the 
recommendations made by the National Development Council. That is one 
thing. 
Then, there is the Inter-State Council. It also considers. The third is that 
there are certain other issues which he  has read out. Now, on the deployment 
of Union Forces in the States under article 355, discussions have taken place and 
people have expressed their views differently. They are at tangent with each other. 
Sometimes, it is said that the Government of India has the authority to deploy 
the forces even without invitation in any State to control disturbances in the 
State. At the same time, others have said that this kind of authority is not 
available to the Government of

is allowed in domestic airlines. However, the Aircraft Rules, 1937 stipulate that a 
Scheduled or Non-Scheduled Air Transport Operator's Permit can be granted only to a 
citizen of India or a company/ body corporate, provided, inter alia, that its

SHRI KAMAL NATH: Sir, I have not answered parts (a) and (b) of the question

citizen of India or to a company/body corporate provided inter alia that substantial and

Eradication of rural poverty 
*407. SHRI URKHAO GWRA BRAHMA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any long term measures for total 
eradication of rural poverty of the country; 
(b) if so, the target year, if any; 
(c) what is the actual figure of rural poverty in India today; 
 
(d) whether such figure is higher in STs and SCs than other communities; 
and 
(e) if so, Government's plan to tackle the problem? 
THE MINISTER OF RURAL DEVELOPMENT (DR. RAGHUVANSH 
PRASAD SINGH): (a) to (e) The Government is committed to eradicate rural 
poverty. To achieve this, the Government has adopted a three pronged 
strategy for reducing poverty in the country. It comprises (i) accelerated 
economic growth with a focus on sect ors which are employment intensive; 
(ii) human and social development through provision of basic minimum 
services; and (iii) targeted anti-poverty programmes. The Tenth Five Year Plan 
envisaged that if the GDP growth target of 8 per cent per annum were attained, 
the poverty ratio would be reduced by 5 percentage points by 2007 and 15 
percentage points by 2012. 
2. Planning Commission estimates poverty at national and State level from 
the large sample survey on 'Household Consumer Expenditure' conducted by 
the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO) at an interval of 
approximately five years. According to the latest such survey conducted during 
1999-2000 (55th Round), the number of persons living below the poverty line in 
the rural areas of the country was 193.2 million (27.09 per cent of the total 
persons living below the poverty line). It is estimated that 36.25 percentage of 
Scheduled Castes and 45.86 percentage of the Scheduled Tribes live below the 
poverty line in rural areas. 
3. In order to improve the living conditions of the rural poor and to uplift 
them above the poverty line, the Government in the Ministry of Rural 
Development is implementing two major employment generation schemes namely 
Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) and Sampoorna 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY). The Government have also launched a new 
wage employment scheme namely National Food For Works Programme 
(NFFWP) in 150 most backward districts of 27 States of the country in order to 
generate supplementary wage employment and to provide food security 
through creation of need based economic, social and community assets in 
these districts. NFFWP is open to the rural poor who are in need of wage 
employment and desire to do manual unskilled work. To provide employment 
in the rural areas to the needy, a comprehensive Bill known as "National Rural 
Employment Guarantee Bill" has been recently framed and introduced in the 
Parliament. 
4. The SGSY particularly focuses on vulnerable groups among the rural 
poor. Guidelines stipulate that the SCs/STs will account for atleast 50% of the 
Swarozgaris assisted, and that the subsidy provided to the SC/STs persons 
would also be at a higher rate of 50% of the project cost subject to a maximum 
of Rs. 10,000/. Under the Sampooma Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), 
22.5% of the resources given to each District and intermediate-level panchayat 
must be spent on individual beneficiary/ group schemes for SCs/STs below the 
poverty line. Besides, out of the earmarked resources at Gram Panchayat level a 
minimum of 50% share of the resources is meant for creation of need-based 
village infrastructure in SC/ST habitations/wards. Under the National Food 
For Works Programme (NFFWP), 150 most backward districts were 
identified by the Planning Commission on the basis of proportion of SC/ST 
population, agricultural productivity per worker and agricultural wage rates 
ensuring due preference for the SC/ST population.

New norms to be set by WTO on anti-dumping duties 
2980. SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in the forthcoming WTO negotiations, WTO is going to set 
new norms on anti-dumping duties; 
(b) if so, whether the new norms will whittle duty protection that is available to 
India on anti-dumping duties; 
(c) how Government is going to deal with it in the WTO Conference; 
(d) whether any strategy has been prepared for this purpose; and 
56 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) and (d) Negotiations have been 
undergoing since November 2001 under the Doha Work Programme, including in 
the area of WTO Rules inter alia aimed at clarifying and improving disciplines 
under the Agreement on Implementation of Article VI of the GATT 1994 
(commonly known as Anti-Dumping Agreement), white preserving the basic 
concepts, principles and effectiveness of this Agreement and its instruments 
and objectives, and taking into accoun t the needs of developing and least-
developed participants. 
The negotiations are being undertaken in the Negotiating Group on Rules 
set up by the Trade Negotiations Committee in 2002 and are aimed at clarifying 
and improving disciplines under the Anti-dumping Agreement. Negotiations are 
still ongoing. 
(c) to (e) In the initial phase of th e negotiations, participants indicated 
provisions, including disciplines on trade distorting practices, that they seek to 
clarify and improve in the subsequent phase. Many WTO members have 
submitted formal proppsals seeking clarification and/or improving disciplines on 
different aspects of anti-dumping agreement in the Negotiating Group on Rules. 
However, a full clarity on possible outcome has yet to emerge Our negotiating 
objectives and strategies have been developed based on analytical work and a 
process of dialogue with relevant stakeholders. India is actively engaged in the 
negotiations and in this regard has also submitted certain proposals to the 
Negotiating Group on Rules on different aspects of the Anti-Dumping 
Agreement. As negotiations intensify in the run up to next WTO Ministerial 
Conference in December 2005, India will remain actively engaged in these 
negotiations to ensure that its interests and concerns continue to be adequately 
addressed as negotiations proceed from one stage to the next. India seeks a 
balanced outcome in the Rules negotiations in line with the Doha mandate.

Demand of India on farm sectc at WTO meeting 
2997. SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) what are the specific duties that India is going to demand on a farm sector 
in the forthcoming WTO meeting; 
(b) what exactly is the meaning of Red Box, Blue Box, Amber Box and Green 
Box; and 
(c) why India is allowed to put some of its things in Green Box? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI E.V.K.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) In the on-going 
negotiations on the World Trade Organisation (WTO) Agreement on 
Agriculture, the July 2004 Framework Agreement provides that the tariff 
reductions will be made by Members from the bound rates on the basis of a 
tiered formula. Special and differential treatment for developing countries, 
including through longer implementation periods, will be integral to all aspects of 
the market access pillar, and the Framework Agreement also provides that the 
tariff reduction commitments of developing Members will be proportionately 
lower than those of developed Members. The G-20, of which India is a 
member, has proposed straight linear cuts within each tier of the tariff 
reduction formula. The tiered formula and other aspects of tariff reductions 
are under negotiation. The negotiations are expected to conclude by 
December 2006. 
(b) Under the WTO Agreement on Agriculture subsidies are generally 
identified by coloured "boxes": Amber (meant to be reduced), Blue (meant to limit 
production), Green (permitted). Though  the Agreement has no Red Box, 
export subsidies exceedi ng the commitments speci fied in a Member's 
Schedule, and domestic support exceeding the reduction commitment levels 
in the Amber Box, are prohibited. 
All domestic support measures that distort production and trade fall into the 
Amber Box, which is defined in Article 6 of the Agreement, and include 
measures to support prices, or subsidies directly related to production 
quantities. These Amber Box support measures are subject 
74 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to limits: "de minimis" minimal supports are allowed (up to 5% of total 
agricultural production for developed countries, and 10% for developing 
countries). Amber, Box expressed in terms of "Total Aggregate 
Measurement of Support", was required to be reduced by 20% for developed 
countries in 6 years (1995-2000) and by 13.33% for developing countries in 10 
years (1995-2004) in equal annual instalments. 
Any domestic support that would normally be in the Amber Box, is placed 
in the Blue Box if the support also requires farmers to limit production under 
Article 6.5 of the Agreement. At present there are no ceilings on spending on 
Blue Box subsidies. 
The Green Box is defined in Annex 2 of the Agreement, and in order to 
qualify, Green Box subsidies must have either no, or at most minimal, trade-
distorting effects or effects on production, and must be government funded Green 
Box subsidies are allowed without limit also provided they meet policy-specific 
criteria set out in Annex 2, and include regional development and 
environment protection and direct income support programmes that are not 
targeted at particular products. 
(c) India, like all WTO Members, is allowed to provide subsidies to its 
agricultural sector provided the government funded programmes meet the 
criteria set out in Annex 2 of the WT O Agreement on Agriculture and such 
subsidies are accounted for as those falling within the Green Box.

gearing up of public grievances redressal system and creation of Local 
Resistance Groups.

of insurgency and naxalism, which inter alia include deployment of Army 
and Central Paramilitary Forces, coordi nated action by the security forces

Central force to assist the people during disasters 
3069. SHRI S. ANBALAGAN: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the Central Government propose to raise an exclusive Central force to 
assist/serve the people during the relief and rescue operations immediately after the 
natural calamities such as earthquake, flood and Tsunami; 
(b) if so, the details thereof and the time by when this force is likely to be raised; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether such an exclusive/specially trained force would be of much help in assisting 
the people during natural calamities; and 
(e) if so, the steps proposed to be taken by the Central Government in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI S. 
REGUPATHY): (a) to (e) Based on the lessons learnt from the past, there has been a 
change in the disaster management policy orientation in India from a relief centric 
approach to a holistic multi-disciplinary and multi-sectoral approach encompassing all 
the elements of disaster management i.e. prevention, mitigation preparedness, 
response, relief and rehabilitation. The approach emanates from the conviction that 
development can not be sustained unless disaster mitigation and preparedness are built 
into the developmental process. In line with the recent change in approach the 
Government of India have taken several measures to strengthen our response 
capabilities. In this context, the Government of India has introduced the Disaster 
Management Bill, 2005 in the Rajya Sabha. The Bill inter alia provides for 
strengthening the existing disaster management mechanism in the country, which would 
facilitate a holistic, coordinated and prompt response to natural calamities. The Bill also 
provides for Constitution of National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) for specialized 
response to any natural calamities. Eight battalions of Central Paramilitary Forces have 
been earmarked to constitute NDRF. Each of these battalions will have 18 specialist 
Search and Rescue teams. The process of training and equipping of specialized terms of 
the NDRF battalions has already begun. 
136 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
The State Governments/UT Administrations have also been advised to 
constitute Search and Rescue teams for immediate response and assistance to 
the people affected by natural calamities. The State/UTs have been authorized 
to procure necessary equipment for Search and Rescue teams under Calamity 
Relief Fund (CRF).

bridge collapse at the Teesta Low Dam Hydel Project due to inherent 
environmental hazards; 
(b) what is the rationale of building dams over unpredictable glacier-fed 
Himalayan rivers flowing through highly seismic and unstable rock 
formations; and 
(c) whether India has any standing pact with China for constant 
monitoring of water levels of rivers in Tibet due to glacial-bursts? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P.M. SAYEED): (a) The causes for 
recent shut-down of Nathpa Jhakri Hydro-electric Project (1500 MW) on river 
Sutlej in Himachal Pradesh are heavy rains and flash floods in Sutlej river due 
to breach in Parechu Lake in Tibet. This also caused abrupt rise in silt content 
in the river water much more than the permissible limit of 5000 PPM because of 
which the machines had to be closed down as a precautionary measure to protect 
them from getting damaged. The bridge which collapsed at Teesta Low Dam 
Project Stage-Ill was a temporary bridge and was being dismantled. 
(b) Hydro power projects are built after conducting detailed Hydrological and

the design of structures.

Unbundling of SEBs 
3097. SHRI R. KAMARAJ: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government had decided to extend the deadline by six 
months for unbundling of 11 State Electricity Boards; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
166 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) whether Government has asked the State Governments to deal sternly 
with cases of power theft; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI P. M. SAYEED): (a) and (b) 
Section 172 (a) of the Electricity Ac t, 2003 provides that the State 
Government may, by notification, authorize the State Electricity Board (SEB) 
to continue to function as the State Transmission Utility or a licensee for such 
further-period beyond the period of one year of the provisions of the Act coming 
into force, as may be mutually decided by the Central Government and the 
State Government. 
Nine States are yet to reorganize their SEBs. These States have, from time to 
time, sent proposals to the Central Government for extension of time for the 
reorganization of their respective SEBs. Besides this, Assam and Madhya 
Pradesh also requested for continuation of their respective SEBs only for trading 
purpose. Details of the time period agreed to by the Central Government for these 
States is given in Statement (See below). 
(c) and (d) The Electricity Act, 2003 has stringent provisions to check theft 
of electricity. The National Electricit y Policy states that the States and 
distribution utilities should ensure effective implementation of these provisions 
of the Act and set up Special Courts. It lays emphasis on implementation of 
modern information technology systems by the utilities on a priority basis, after 
considering cost and benefits, to facilitate creation of network information and 
customer data base which will inter-alia, help in detection of theft and 
tampering. High Voltage Distribution System has also been envisaged in the 
policy as an effective method for prevention of theft as well as reduction of 
technical losses, improved voltage profile and better consumer service. 
The Electricity Rules, 2005 prescribe the procedure for investigation of 
congnizable offences related to thef t of electricity by the Police. The  
Electricity (Removal of Difficulties) Order, 2005 issued by Central 
Government under section 183 of the Act provides that the Electricity Supply 
Code as specified by the SERCs under section 50 of the Act shall also include 
method of assessment of electricity charges and  disconnection of supply in 
cases of theft of electricity pending adjudication by the appropriate court.

Watershed Management Programme 
3103. DR. GYAN PRAKASH PILANIA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of the Watershed Management Programme; 
(b) the areas and extent of coverage of this programme in Rajasthan; 
(c) whether any survey has been done to ascertain the success of this programme; 
and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA): (a) The Department of Land 
Resources in the Ministry of Rural Development is implementing three 
174 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Area Development Programmes, namely  Integrated Wasteland Development 
Programme (IWDP), Drought Prone Areas Programme (DPAP) and Desert 
Development Programme (DDP) for development of wastelands, drought 
proofing and checking desertification on watershed basis in the country w.e.f. 
1.4.1995. Presently, DPAP is under implementation in 972 blocks of 182 
districts in 16 States and DDP is being implemented in 235 blocks in 40 
districts of 7 States. The projects under IWDP are generally sanctioned in 
areas other than DPAP/DDP areas. The project period of watershed 
development projects is generally 4-5 years. The focus of these programmes 
is to ensure efficient land and water resource management for sustainable 
production. These programmes are implemented with the involvement of 
local people in planning and execution of works on watershed basis. To 
empower Panchayat Raj Institutions (PRIs), Government of India issued the 
Hariyati Guidelines w.e.f. 01.04.2003 for implementation of DPAP, DDP and 
IWDP watershed programmes. Funding of projects under these programmes 
is shared between Centre and State in ratio of 75:25 in case of DPAP/ DDP 
and 11:1 in IWDP. From 1.4.1995 till 31.3.2005,885 IWDP projects for 
treatment of an area of 61.97 lakh ha. at a total cost of Rs. 3351.97 crores 
have been sanctioned, out of which Rs . 1310.43 crores have been released. 
Under DPAP, 21353 projects have been sanctioned for treatment of 106.77 
lakh ha. at a total cost of Rs. 5569.20 crores, out of which Rs. 1742.40 crores 
have been released. Under DDP, 11476 projects for 57.38 lakh ha. have been 
sanctioned at a total cost of Rs. 3074.40, out of which Rs. 1301.01 crores 
have been released. 
(b) From 1.4.1995 till 31.3.2005, 59 IWDP projects in 22 districts for 
treatment of 3.71 lakh ha. at a total cost of Rs. 209.29 crores have been 
sanctioned to the State of Rajasthan and Rs. 91.23 crores have been released 
as central share. Under DPAP, 872 projects have been sanctioned and Rs. 
89.34 crores have been released. Under DDP, 5303 projects have been 
sanctioned and Rs. 13.01 crores have been released. 
(c) and (d) Yes, Sir. Impact assessment studies conducted in 26 districts of 
Rajasthan show that the net sown area in the State of Rajasthan has increased 
by 12% across the State. On an averag e, in each watershed, the number of 
dug wells increased from 26 to 30, tubewells from 11 to 14, ponds from 2 to 
5, mainstreams with moisture from 10 to 17. The water level in wells has 
also increased from average of 44.5 m depth 
175 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
to 42.06 m depth. The command area under various sources of irrigation also 
increased. The average area under tree and vegetation has increased in all the 
watershed areas with increased fodder  availability in all the watershed 
development programmes. Over 19.2 million man-days were generated under 
these programmes in 12 districts at an average of 0.25 million man-days per 
watershed.

Year Plan— Contd. 
MR. CHAIRMAN: How much time would you require, Mr. Minister?

SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Mr. Chairman Sir, hon. Member, Shri 
Sitaram Yechury, and others have raised important issues regarding the recent 
slowdown in the growth rate of agriculture sector and its impact on poverty and 
unemployment, in the course of the discussion regarding the Mid-Term Appraisal. 
I would only like to point out that the Government is sensitive to the issues raised by 
them, and that a comprehensive policy and plan of action in regard to many of 
the points raised by the hon. Members has been appropriately incorporated in 
the Mid-Term Appraisal of the Tenth Five Year Plan.

SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN: Sir, our senior colleague and hon. 
Minister for Agriculture, Shri Sharad Pawar, has responded to many of the 
concerns, which had been raised by the hon. Members yesterday. Therefore, I 
would not like to go into those things again. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
However, Sir, I would like to point out that planning in India has always 
focussed on removal of poverty, unemployment and raising the growth in 
agricultural production as core concerns. Consequently, apart from raising growth 
rate in the economy, a number of anti-poverty and employment generation 
programmes have been launched from time to time. 
In recent years, the growth rates have increased significantly. The rate of 
growth of GDP during the period 1951-81 was close to 3.6 per cent per 
annum, whereas from 1981 to 2001, the rate of growth was 5.6 per cent. The 
latter period has also seen substantial reduction in the proportion of persons 
living below poverty line, from nearly 45 per cent in 1983 to 26 per cent in 1999-
2000. Reduction in the poverty ratio is being attributed, among other factors, to 
the acceleration in growth rates. 
An important question that the Tenth Five Year Plan addresses is, how 
could the growth rate be accelerated as well as structured so as to achieve even 
faster reduction in poverty levels. Although growth has strong and direct poverty-
reducing effects, friction and rigidities in the economy could make these 
processes less effective. The Tenth Plan is, therefore, formulated in a manner, 
which explicitly addresses the need to ensure 
200 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
equity and social justice. The composition of growth is important. It has 
been found that agricultural productivity and public expenditure on social 
development have stronger poverty-reducing effects than other 
components of growth. 
The growth and poverty reduction approach integrates four main 
components. Firstly, agricultural development is viewed as a core element 
of the Plan since growth in this sector is likely to lead to the widest spread 
of benefits, especially to the rural poor. In this context, it is recognized in 
the Mid-Term Appraisal that policie s facilitating agricultural growth 
including land reforms and watershed development are crucial. I would 
not elaborate on the agricultural sector, Sir; as I have pointed out, the 
hon. Minister of Agriculture, Shri Sharad Pawar, has already responded 
to some of the concerns expressed by the hon. Members. However, Sir, 
I would like to say a few words on the availability and management of 
water, which our hon. friend, Shri Sitaram Yechury, has pointed out and 
he especially drawn the attention with  regard to irrigation, which is an 
important constraint for raising the growth rate of agriculture sector. In 
this connection, the priorities laid down in the Mid-Term Appraisal are 
completion of on-going irrigation projec ts; rehabilitation of the existing 
irrigation systems; ground-water development in areas where there is 
unutilised potential through back-ended subsidy schemes; artificial 
recharge of ground water in areas suffering from aquifer depletion; and 
inclusion of command area development works as part of major and 
medium projects. States should set up Water Regulators for periodically 
revising water tariffs. The States could also set up Water Users' 
Associations to manage distribution of water and also empower them to 
collect the tariff, and retain a part of it for system maintenance. 
Programmes for the treatment of  wastelands and degraded lands, 
including steps at water conservation are extremely important for rain-
fed areas and should be implemented by single Department or Agency 
along with community participation. 
Sir, Shri Sitaram Yechury, the hon. Member, mentioned that water tariffs 
should not be increased, but I would like to point out, with all my humility 
at my command, that without this, it would not be possible to carry out 
proper operations and maintenance of irrigation works in the country, nor 
will it be possible to pass on the responsibility of irrigation to water user's 
associations. 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
Moreover, agricultural development is not only about irrigation and 
direct investment in agriculture. It should be recognized that success in 
this area depends critically upon the development of other essential 
infrastructure in rural areas including especially development of transport 
linkages, rural electrification and, in the case of exports, suitable handling 
facilities at airports. Therefore, Sir, the Bharat Nirman has been conceived 
during the current year for building infrastructure with specific targets for 
completion in four years. Sir, I would like to draw the kind attention of the 
hon. Member about the announcement made recently as far as Bharat 
Nirman is concerned. The UPA Government in the coming four years is 
going to spend Rs. 1,74,000 crore in taking care of various programmes 
which need to be taken into consideration to improve the quality of life of 
the poorer section of our people. As far as the components are concerned, 
there are six components, namely, irrigation, roads, water supply, housing, 
rural electrification and rural telecom connectivity. In irrigation, it is 
proposed to provide assured irrigation to 1 crore hectare additional area, 
which will give a big boost to agriculture and thereby improving the quality 
of life of the poorer section of the people, particularly agricultural labourer. 
The Union Government is already assisting the States to complete last 
mile irrigation projects through t he Accelerated Irrigation Benefits 
Programme, which is known as AIBP. The outlays for AIBP have been 
stepped up from Rs.2800 crore in 2004-05 to Rs.4500 crore for 2005-06. 
Depending on the response from States, it is proposed to further step up 
AIBP in the coming years as a part of funding Bharat Nirman. 
In addition to the revival of agricultural growth, the MTA aims at attaining 
rapid growth in sectors, which have a large employment potential. These 
include sectors such as construction, tourism, transport, small-scale 
industry, modern retailing, IT sector to enable services and a range of 
other new services, which need to  be promoted through supportive 
policies. In order to supplement the impact of growth, specific programmes 
aimed at special target groups and building safety nets which have all 
along been part of Indian development strategy, are being strengthened 
to ensure that they are effective in achieving their objectives. The 
Government is implementing several anti-poverty programmes, both in 
the rural and urban areas also. In fact, yesterday, you were kind enough 
to refer as to what is going to happen to the urban poor. Now, this point 
has been taken very well. Shri Sharad Pawar, hon. Minister of Agriculture, 
202 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
has already mentioned about the Food-for-Work Programme and the 
Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme. However, at the national level, 
there are other schemes which also need to be mentioned here. 
The Swaranjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY) has the objective 
of bringing assisted poor families above the poverty line by organising 
them into Self Help Groups (SHGs) through the process of social 
mobilisation, their training and capacity building and provision of income 
generating assets through a mix of Bank credit and Government subsidy. 
The SGSY programme is conceived as a process oriented programme 
for the poor with emphasis on social mobilisation and formation of SHGs. 
I am sure our hon. Member, Shrimati Brinda Karat, would be happy to 
know that in this category, lakhs of Self-Help Groups have come into 
being and the Finance Minister has made an announcement on the floor 
of the House that needed credit system is going to be provided specially 
directed towards the Self-Help Groups particularly managed by woman 
members. 
Sir, the Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) aims to provide 
additional wage employment in all rural areas and thereby provide food 
security and improved nutritional levels. The Secondary objective is the 
creation of durable community, social and economic assets and 
infrastructural development in rural areas. The SGRY is open to all rural 
poor who are in need of wage employment and desire to do manual and 
unskilled work in and around the village or whatever habitat they are 
residing. 
As far as urban poverty is concerned, I would like to draw the kind 
attention of hon. Member, Shri Yechuryji, that the Swarna Jayanti Shahari 
Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY) aims to provide gainful employment through 
setting up of self-employment ventures or provision of wage employment. 
This is a demand-driven scheme, however, an annual target of 80,000 
under self-employment including subsidy sub-component, and one lakh 
persons under training sub-component has been fixed. 
It is also recognised that poverty and unemployment exhibit regional 
concentration which needs to be addressed. Efforts are being made to 
reduce inter-regional disparities through greater focus on growth in 
backward States and regions in order to promote balanced regional 
development. The Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana (RSVY) was launched to

Demand to scrap black list of Sikh protestors maintained by 
Indian embassies abroad 
SHRI TARLOCHAN SINGH (Haryana): Sir, I want the raise to problem 
of non issue of visas to people of Indian origin, specially the Sikhs, by our 
embassies. It is a well-known fact that all over the world Sikhs held protest 
marches to express their anger against the Army attack on the Golden 
Temple, Amritsar in 1984. The Indian Embassies put the names of all 
those protestors in a Black List; and since then they have disallowed 
them to visit their places of birth in India. For the last 21 years, this Black 
List has been in existence. These NRIs are not allowed to visit their aged 
parents, or, to attend the social function of their relatives. The Government 
221 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
of India has recently decided to grant dual citizenship to NRIs. But we 
fail to understand this policy of the Home Ministry to deprive the above-
mentioned category of persons merely because they took part in 
demonstrations outside the embassies in 1984. It is high time we scrap 
the Black List and allow them to visit their ancestral villages here. The 
Government can grant temporary visas to those who are still considered 
to be in the category of people under suspicion. With my experience, I 
can say that anyone who visits Punjab definitely goes back fully satisfied 
with the local situation there. We can win them over by showing them a 
peaceful and progressing Punjab. By refusing them visas, the Government 
is encouraging a powerful group in the West which can be exploited by 
anti-India lobby. 
The Government may also help thousands of Indian youth who are 
living in many Western countries in order to get them citizenship of those 
countries. They are badly in need of some documents which can easily 
be provided by our Embassies. Many countries, especially in Europe, 
have recently changed their in migrat ion laws to have thousands of 
persons for specific jobs. Because of the non-cooperative attitude of our 
Embassies, many non-Indian illegal migrants are availing themselves of 
these opportunities. The Indian Government should come forward to help 
our youth who have gone there by some means to get employment.

Concern over the recommendation to outsource all key 
operations in F.C.I. 
SHRI G.K. VASAN (Tamil Nadu): Si r, it has been reported in the 
newspapers that a multi-national consultancy company has recommended 
reduction of workforce in the Food Corporation of India by outsourcing all 
key operations like foodgrains proucement, handling, transportation and 
distribution as part of the restructing plan of FCI. The operations done by 
its regular staff including head-loaders are sought to be outsourced, if it 
is so, I would strongly oppose the anti-labour policy of the Government in 
the name of saving the operational costs in FCI. 
222 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Sir, the Food Corporation of India has been mandated to function as 
the lifeline of public distribution system which serves the poor and the 
deprived section of the country. It has been performing a very important 
public distribution function thus ensuring the food security of the country 
on the one hand, and also ensuring that our farmers are not exploited on 
the other. It is disturbing to note that the Government is silently examining 
the report of the multi-national consultancy firm on revamping of the FCI 
structure. 
Any measures to achieve fiscal prudence should not overlook the 
humanitarian aspect of rendering thousands of workers jobless. I urge 
the Government to abandon this anti-labour move at the behest of a 
report of a multi-national consultant whose interest is to bring in MNCs 
and other foreign grain dealers to the Indian market place.

Havoc caused by flood in certain parts of Karnataka 
SHRI JANARDHANA POOJAY (Karnataka) Sir, as the august House 
is aware, Karnataka State is fa cing calamitous situation following 
unprecedented rainfall and flood in nineteen districts in the State, 
particularly in Belgaum, Bijapur, Bagalkot, Gulbarga, Raichurand Dakshin 
Kannada districts. 
The deluge has inundated 115 villages, left 126 dead, perished over 
11,610 cattle, damaged 85,601 houses, completely destroyed crop spread 
over 4 lakh acres and extensively damaged roads, bridges, houses, power 
and water supply systems in 1, 290 villages. 
I thank Smt. Sonia Gandhji, hon. UPA Chairpersons, Dr. Manmohan 
Singhji, hon. Prime Minister of India and Shri Sharad Pawarji, hon. Union 
Minister of Agriculture, for visiting the State to personally appraise the 
situation, console the victims and announce a total grant of Rs. 400 crores 
to the State to help it meet the challenges. 
The Scale and magnitude of the havoc caused by the torrential rain 
and floods demand extensive relief and rehabilitation measures, both 
223 

RAJYA SABHA [24 A ugust, 2005] 
immediate and long-term. A minimum of Rs. 1,500 crores would be required 
for the purpose. Therefore, the Centre may kindly consider (1) releasing 
immediately Rs. 1,500 crores to facilitate Karnataka to implement the 
relief and rehabilitation works; and (2) grant some credit and relief package to 
the affected farmers through banks.

Demand to introduce Metro Rail Service in Tamil Nadu 
SHRIC. PERUMAL (Tamil Nadu): Sir, Tamil Nadu is the second most 
urbanised State in the country, next only to Maharashtra. Its capital, 
Chennai, is the fourth city in the country. Chennai is not only a gateway to 
Southern Indian but also an international city. Many multi-national companies 
have set up their offices here. The population of Chennai has already crossed 75-
lakh mark. Added to this, about to lakh persons visit Chennai everyday. The traffic 
in the city has increased manifold. Moreover, there is no scope for expansion of the 
city. There is no scope for expansion of roads or construction of new roads. 
Moreover, even if it is considered to lay new roads, there will be dislocation of 
offices, colleges and schools and they may be damaged, in the metropolitan 
cities of the world and also in the National Capital Territory of Delhi, with a view to 
managing the ever-growing traffic, metro rail system and tramways have been 
introduced and functioning successfully. In Chennai, we already have suburban 
train system and no problem in laying metro rail and tram. 
Likewise, Madurai is the second largest city in Tamil Nadu. It is an 
important tourist centre and thousands of foreigners come here everyday, many 
large industrial houses have set their offices here. Coimbatore is also an 
important commercial centre. It has thousands of manufacturing units and also 
one of the important textile centres in the country. The population of Madurai 
and Coimbatore has already crossed 15 lakhs. 
Therefore, I urge upon the Government to introduce metro rail system in 
Chennai, Madurai and Coimbatore and tramways in Chennai at the earliest.

Demand for the establishment of Maritime University at 
Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, the Ministry of 
Shipping is envisaging the need for establishment of two Maritime

Universities-one in the East Coast and one in the West Coast- in India. 
Sir, Visakhapatnam is an ideal location for the Maritime University on the 
East Coast due to following reasons: 
1. Andhra Pradesh is having the longest coastine of 980 kms. among 
the East coast maritime States and studded with 12 State ports. 
2. Visakhapatnam is ideally and centrally located in the East Coast of 
India. 
3. Dredging Corporation of India is located and operated for 
Visakhapatnam. 
Sir, Maritime Engineering course has been introduced in Andhra 
University around 1968 and produced a number of maritime engineers. 
The Eastern Naval Command Head Quarters, the Hindustan Shipyard, 
the National Ship Design and Research Centre and the Regional Centre 
of the National Institute of Oceanography are located at Visakhapatnam. 
The Government of Andhra pradesh has also expressed its willingness 
to provide the necessary land for t he establishment of the Maritime 
University at Visakhapatnam. 
Hence, I request the Government of India to expedite the process of 
establishment of Maritime University at Visakhapatnam. Thank you.

SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE (Maharashtra): Sir, I am grateful to 
you for this opportunity. Sir, I have the onerous task of responding to this 
flamboyantly eloquent assault, which was really a relentless assault, almost like 
a pre-emptive strike, with some rational approach. Sir, we are here to discuss 
the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2005 as passed by the Lok 
Sabha. Sir probably, with his speech, the hon. Minister wanted this House to 
pass the Bill without discussion. But it is not going to be so. This House is 
going to discuss the Bill. 
Sir, we are going through this legislation and we are in the process of 
passing it in a kind of tearing haste, and almost by habit, I find that when you 
talk about haste, acting in haste, you always are apprehensive of repenting 
in leisure. 
So, this tearing haste should not, I hope, lead us to repentance because this 
haste is reflected in the formulation and the passage of this Bill. ""&. ?i«i ^1 ^m 
aflr w ^ra ^Jt ^pft" was the dream put forward by Shri Deen Dayal Upadhaya 
40 years ago, and that has been the cherished dream of this country. But, Sir, 
today we are not discussing dreams only, but we are also passing a law which 
will create certain enforceable rights and certain obligatory liabilities. Sir, any 
Government functions through certain policies and through its law-making. 
Both are the functions of the Government. But, there is a qualitative 
difference between the two. In so far as the Government's policy is concerned, 
it is a matter of expression of intent. And, if it is exposed, you find that 
expression of intent was hollow. I have the example of the National Education 
Policy of 1986 which formulated the universalisation of education, and, I believe, in 
the Planning Commission, at that moment, the relevant Member (Education) 
was Prof. M.G.K. Menon, who said, "We don't have even a pie for this project". 
So, 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
a policy formulation was there and there was failure. But, sir, when you enact 
a statute, it is a commitment of Parliament to the people. A statute is not 
merely a commitment, but it creates enforceable rights for the people. 
Therefore, everybody has to think more while passing a law, because it is 
supposed to be implemented. When I was referring to the National 
Education Policy, I was reminded of an axiomatic saying by Prof. D.S. 
Kothari, who produced the earlier Education Commission Report. He said 
that a report is no substitute to an action. Therefore, a dream brought on 
paper is no substitute for an action. And, I believe that the present legislation is 
fated to be disillusionment because (i) there was no homework, (ii) there 
was no ground assessment and, (iii) there was no understanding of a future 
prospective. Therefore, I am afraid, at the implementation level, this legislation 
is facing a darker future. Sir, in so far as the homework is concerned, I find 
firstly that the bulk of the legislation is on the basis of implementation by the 
States, and States are, at no stage, involved in the making of this law. They are 
not involved; they are not consulted. It was clear when the Secretaries of the 
States gave evidence before the Standing Committee. Without their 
involvement, this legislation can't be successful and they are not involved at any 
stage so far. 
Secondly, Sir, the financial implication ought to have been studied 
beforehand. But that has not been done. Wherefrom the money will come? 
Nobody knows it. Even the Finance Minister does not know. He says, "we 
will find money somewhere". In such circumstances, Sir, it is always said if your 
conclusions are wrong, check your premises. 
In the present scheme of things, the premises are that there is 
unemployment there are finances, a nd, therefore, employment is 
guaranteed. But here it is the other way round. What kind of unemployment is 
there, is not assessed. From where will the finances come? Nobody knows. 
And, therefore, I believe, the conclusion is that there is no guarantee of 
getting employment. 
(ii) Secondly, sir, there is no ground assessment before passing this 
legislation. Today, there are several schemes working. In fact, there is a long 
list. And the physical performance-of these schemes- is noted by the 
Economic Survey of 2004-05. The National Food-for-work Programme was 
started in November, 2004, in which Rs. 2,020 crores were invested and 
twenty lakh tonnes of foodgrains were made available. The 
244 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
Swarnajayanti Gram Swarojgar Yojana (SGSY)-the bureaucrats talks in 
these terminologies, SGSY or SGRY, which I do not understand 
immediately-was initiated in April, 1999. The Sampooma Grameen Rojgar 
Yojana (SGRY) was initiated in 2001; it was to be implemented through 
Panchayati Raj institutions. Then  the Rural Employment Generation 
Programme (REGP) was initiated in 1995, and the Report says that 8.32 lakh 
jobs were created up to 2003-04, and 5.25 lakh jobs were to be created 
during 2004-05. Then there is the Prime Minister's Rojgar Yojana (PMRY), 
which was initiated in 1993. Under it, self-employment units so far, are 20 
lakhs, and the target for 2004-05 was 16.50 lakh employment opportunities. 
The Swarnajayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana (SJSRY) was initiated in 1997, 
and the Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) was initiated in 1993. 
Sir, apart from these, there are several other schemes for rural 
development which essentially are the schemes for rural employment. What 
is the yield of all these schemes? What is the correlation between the money 
spent and the employment generated? And then, what remains to be done? 
Nobody has studied it. And, Sir, if these or any of these schemes have 
failed, and inquiry is necessary as to why it has failed. If the earlier schemes 
has failed due to certain reasons, without eradicating those reasons, any 
scheme for rural employment is bound to fail. Therefore, I am saying that no 
ground assessment is made before going into this legislation. 
Sir, I remember, every year when a Railway Minister presents his 
Budget, he sanctions several schemes, and then certain allocation is made 
for each of those schemes. If there are several Ministers within a period of 5-
6 years, then so many schemes are sanctioned. Each schemes is given certain 
amount of money. Therefore, there are 100 projects pending—100 projects 
at a stage where some money is spent, much more is to be spent, and they 
continue to be pending. We have scores of such examples in any report of the 
Railway Convention Committee. Sir, if there are already 10-20 schemes, and 
one more scheme is going to be added to these; some money is spent on 
the earlier schemes without results, some more money will be spent on the 
scheme without results; and therefore, we will be having schemes but no 
results. 
(iii) The third congenital defect in this  legislation is that there is no 
understanding, no assessment of a future perspective. What projects

In these projects, how many people will be employed? When the 
Ministry was asked, the Ministry said that the data in so far as people above 
the poverty line are concerned, is not maintained. So, there is no data. This 
makes everything vague, everything doubtful and doesn't generate 
confidence; there is no question of guarantee. And, Sir, I would like to mention 
here that apart from those who are unemployed, there are ten crore 
agricultural labourers who must be treated almost as unemployed because

Sir, now, I seek to come to the Bill itself and it abounds, again, in defects. 
Sir, only one substantial amendment on the basis of the Standing Committee's 
Report was accepted. It the other amendments proposed were accepted, the 
Bill would have taken a different shape. And that one amendment is from

therefore, all calcuations have gone haywrie. The Financial memorandum is 
based on the concept of every poor household, where they have calculated 
such able-bodied persons to be about ten crore, accumulated in 3.86 
families. I don't find any other word for accumulated, but people belonging 
to 3.86 families. For them, for 100 days, you will require 1,00,464 crores. All 
these calculations are on this and there also, they say we may not be 
required to spend this much because every person doesn't ask for a job. 
Those who demand job may be only fifty per cent. Therefore, we may be 
required to spend only fifty thousand crore. But that calculation is on the basis 
that you have to cater to ten crore. The moment you talk of removing 'poor' in 
every household, then you refer to 38.91 crore of able-bodied persons, not 
only men, between 18 and 64 age group. Where are the calculations for this, 
even the rudimentary calculations? And if 100,464 crore is a tall order, four-
folds of this will be an order of such a nature that you will lose your cap when 
looking up. Therefore, one amendment has put the legislation in a state of 
being haywire.

the fiscal, economics, etc. I just apprise you that I don't think that the financial 
aspect is the most important aspect. That is the second level aspect. When all 
is said and done, over a period of time there would be pressure on the Budget, 
whether it is 30,000,40,000 or 20,000,60,000. That does't matter. But there would 
be a pressure on the Budget. And the most important thing at that point of time 
which I would urge the Minister, and, through him, the Government and the 
Finance Minister is that if we have to make economies anywhere, these 
economies must not be made in areas which are of interest for poverty 
alleviation. 'Education for All', 'Health for All', Irrigation, Public Investment, Water, 
we must protect these poverty alleviation schemes. And, this again, must be an 
assurance from the Government every year that if there is a stress on the Budget, 
we are cutting something else, but not on the poverty alleviation schemes, 
because those poverty alleviation schemes are the final answer, are the ultimate 
answer. The employment guarantee is an interim solution to a problem which 
we are facing. So, this is the second related problem. But let us not worry about 
the money, let us implement it and then make sure that if there is a pressure on 
the Budget, we sacrifice or the cost of it is not borne by the real poverty 
alleviation schemes which provide sustainable employment and sustainable 
output in the long run. Sir, this is the second related point. 
The third and the final point, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, which is slightly 
economic is that I would suggest to the Finance Minister, or, rather through the Rural 
Development Minister to the-Finance Minister that when the stress is 
developed, or whenever it happens, let us not get into new taxes,

THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF P.J. KURIAN): Shri Arjun Sengupta. 
Is it your maiden speech? 
SHRI ARJUN KUMAR SENGUPTA(West Bengal): Yes, it is my maiden 
speech. I feel very proud that I am speaking on this very historic occasion after a 
truly historic Bill has been approved by the Lok Sabha. There are two major 
reasons why this Bill is historic. One is—I think that the point has been made 
by Shri Nilotpal Basu and also earlier by my friend, Dr. Bimal Jalan that this is 
really a consensus Bill. After the Standing Committee's deliberations, the 
original Bill has changed so substantially that it is very difficult for anybody to say 
that all the experiences of the previous programmes have not been considered 
and taken into account. Avery clear example of that was the role of the 
Panchayats. Shri Dhawan pointed it out how the original emphasis of the 
Programme Officer got changed into monitoring, implementation and also 
programme design by the Panchayats. These are all results of discussion that 
took place, 
271 

RAJYA SABHA [24 August, 2005] 
and I think, it is a truly historic Bill in that sense of a consensus. The second 
reason why it is a historic Bill, and this is what I beg to submit to you, is that this 
really means a paradigm shift of economic policy. We are not fully appreciating 
the implication of that. It is, of course, a Bill which is guaranteeing unemployment 
insurance which most industrial countries have in its direct form or direct 
transfer of 100 days work. I think after this, suicide by firmers, etc., will 
become history. It would be available to everybody and everywhere. 
Secondly, it will remove or reduce poverty very significantly. There are 
calculations which show that if only the poor get the benefit of this, poverty 
would have come down by about 40 per cent. But I am not saying that only 
the poor will take advantage of this. In our country, 75 per cent of our people 
live below 2 dollars a days, which is a universal definition of the poverty line. 
So, most of our people are poor. If even somebody above the Indian poverty 
line which is even less than one dollar, can take advantage of this, it will 
make a definite impact on poverty. The third, and I think, the most important 
provision is that this is the first time a right to work has been recognised. Mr. 
Vice-chairman, Sir the language of right has to be fully appreciated. It is not 
just a rhetoric. The American Declaration of Independence said that we, the 
people of the United States, give us this Constitution as our right, and if a 
Government fails to implement that right, we have the right to overthrow that 
Government. The right is a very powerful instrument that is given to the 
people. We are now riding a tiger. If we cannot ride it properly, we shall be 
devoured by the tiger. I think that this is a consensus Bill, and all of us should 
have taken care of this. We must realise our responsibility to see that we do 
deliver. In order to do that, I will just make three points. First is the question of 
cost. Now, there are different estimates of the cost. In fact, most of the cost 
estimates have not taken into account what economists call supply responses. 
People do not go for job just because the salary is available. But estimates 
have been made and that estimates show that—even if it is universal when 
anybody who is willing to work should get a job—the total expenditure would be 
about 2 per cent of the GDP. This is on the basis of their reservation wage, 
as we call, casual workers' wage, etc., compared to different levels of market 
wages. 
But, we do not say that; we say "only people who are really needy", as it 
happened in many places. The Standing Committee talks about 25 per cent 
people, 50 per cent people. Then, the actual amount may be 1.2-1.3

per cent of GDP. Nevertheless,  the total amount would be quite 
substantial,. Let us not fool ourselves that it will be a very small amount. Thirty-
five thousand to fifty thousand crores of rupees is the bill that we should 
actually think of, and if it extends to the urban sector, we should be prepared 
to have another Rs. Ten thousand crores. We may not be able to provide it 
immediately. It has to be done step by step as it has been proposed in the 
Bill and that we should be prepared to provide for that. Now, it is true that for 
seven per cent rate of growth of GDP, this is not much. Two per cent is less 
than one- third of the incremental income. But, it is not true of the Budget. For the 
Budget, it is a very large provision. We have to frame the Budget completely 
differently. We have to consider measures affecting both revenues and 
expenditures. Mr. Jalan pointed out that certain type of expenditures should not 
be cut. He is very correct. You cannot cut expenditure on poverty alleviation if you 
are talking about Employment Guarantee Scheme. Then, you should be 
prepared to adjust your expenditure otherwise, you should also be prepared to 
think about taxes, to think of different ways of raising money. I am quite sure the 
hon. Finance Minister would be able to do that because he knows his arithmetic 
very well. But, it would imply a change of the Budget- making, a change of the 
Budget making, because this is something which cannot be provided by foreign 
aid or investment. You cannot get foreign aid and directly meet the 
requirement because we have to change it into rupees, and if we have to 
change it into rupees, you have to import which is very difficult in these 
circumstances. A new approach to financial management is implied in this 
particular Bill. The second thing is new approach to planning. 
THE VICE-CHAIRMAN (PROF. P.J. KURIAN): Please, be brief. 
SHRI ARJUN KUMAR SENGUPTA: Sir, I want to make two points. The 
point which was mentioned by Shri Apte was very correct. You have to consider 
about what is in the future, and that is planning. You have to now talk about 
schemes in the rural areas, and how they are coordinated with each other, how 
they are balanced with each other in terms of inputs and outputs. This is not the 
plan that we have been following. It is the ground level planning starting from 
below. It is no longer a planning with just a macro-model, worked out at the 
centre. And, third is the decentralisation and I must say that this is the first 
time that Panchayats have been fully involved. Unfortunately, I cannot say that 
tall Panchayats will be able to do this job. They have to be taken through this 
process. A

THE PRIME MINISTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Mr. Chairman, 
Sir, this Bill that is being discussed by this august House is truly in the nature of 
a landmark legislation. It represents a new beginning, a landmark in the regime of 
rights enjoyed by our people, a landmark in our efforts for social equity and 
justice through the provision of social safety nets. Sir, it is a path-breaking 
legislation that entitles our rural poor to a guaranteed employment for a 
defined number of days, a means of sustenance, a means to avert distress, 
a means to secure two square meals a day and a means to lift them out of 
the trap of poverty. It is a commitment that the Congress Party has made to 
the people of this country in its election manifesto which is the culmination of 
several decades of efforts of the Congress, under the Prime Ministership of 
Shrimati Indira Gandhi and Shri Rajiv-Gandhi, to move towards the right to 
livelihood. It is a commitment of the UPA Government to the nation and this 
Legislation demonstration over commitment to the cause of the 
285

poor. Sir, the Government acknowledges the pioneering role of the 
National Advisory Council and Shrimati Sonia Gandhi in drafting this 
Legislation, in maintaining the momentum and pressure required to bring it to 
Parliament speedily and in creating the necessary space for public debate 
which has enabled, in my view, the drafting of a Bill which is 
comprehensive, wide-ranging and most satisfactory few pieces of 
legislations have benefited from a debate, as extensive as this one, which has 
taken place all over our country. Hist ory will remember Soniaji for this 
landmark Legislation, and if this Government is to be remembered for a 
single law or policy, it will be this one. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, why do we need a legislation of this type? It was the dream 
of the founding fathers of our Republic that as India industrialises, more and 
more people will shift out of agriculture and, therefore, industrialisation, by 
and large, should provide a solution to the problem of securing gainful 
livelihood for all our people. We have significant achievements in 
industrialisation. We have today industries in almost every sector of our 
economy. But it is also true that the pace of industrialisation and the pace 
of industrial employment associated with that industrialisation has not been as 
fast as it ought to be. The result is that at the time of Independence, nearly 70 
per cent of our people were living in rural areas. Today, the proportion is no 
less than 60 to 62 per cent. Therefore, employment strategies have to be 
two-fold. We have to accelerate the tempo of industrialisation. We have to 
accelerate the tempo of labour-friendly industrialisation. Therefore, what ever 
comes in the way of speedy industrialisation of our country, in the promotion of 
labour-intensive methods of production and labour-intensive industries can hurt 
this process of creating more job opportunities outside agriculture. 
This has to be the major plank of our Government in the years to come 
and I do hope that the process that we have set in motion in the last 15 years 
will ensure faster and speedier industrialisation of our country. We have still to 
take measures to see that this indus trialisation is as labour-friendly as 
possible. I will come back to that aspect of the problem a little later. At the same 
time, for the people who are living in rural areas, we have to create an 
environment in which their output and employment opportunities can go up. I 
look at the differences between urban India and the rural India at the time of 
independence. They were much narrower than what they are today. So, 
obviously, our rural areas have lagged 
286 

[24 August, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
behind. The development of our agriculture, investment in agriculture, 
investment in new agricultural technologies and ensuring that the small and 
marginal farmers also participate in the processes of the Green Revolution 
have to be an important plank of our strategy for lifting our population out of 
poverty. But we know that about 25 per cent of our population are landless. 
Now, agriculture does offer gainful employment opportunities for a major part of 
the year even for this population. But we all know that once the seasonal peak, 
the sowing and harvesting period, is gone, there is considerable 
unemployment and underemployment in rural areas. We have legislated the 
minimum wage legislation in our country to take care of the landless labour, to 
put a floor on their incomes. But we all know that in rural setting of the type that 
prevails in our country it is very difficult, in practice, to reinforce the minimum 
wage legislation. So, we need strategies to lift the floor of the poorest of the 
poor and employment guarantee is one way to increase the bargaining 
power of the poorest sections of our population, the landless, the Scheduled 
Castes, the Scheduled Tribes and our women. Now, it is certainly true that 
what we are offering to our people is a modest amount, gainful employment 
of 100 days at a minimum wage of Rs. 60 not more than Rs. 500 per 
month for a family. I recognise that this, by itself, is not sufficient. But taking 
into account that most agricultural labour households also get some gainful 
employment during the peak season, the sowing and harvesting period, I do 
believe that this at the margin, will help, in particular, landless families to raise 
their living standards. It will help to provide social safety nets which will protect 
them against the vagaries of unemployment. I sincerely hope that over a 
period of four or five years we will cover all the rural districts of our country. 
That is our solemn commitment. Employment schemes have existed for a 
long number of years. When Indiraji was the Prime Minister, a number of 
employment programmes were devised. Rajivji devised many agricultural 
employment programmes. Similar employment assurance schemes were 
devised when Shri Narasimha Rao was the Prime Minister and I was the 
Finance Minister. There is, however, a cardinal difference. For the first time, 
we are now recognising the right to work as a fundamental legal right. 
Therefore, it casts on all of us in Government and all those who are 
concerned with the processes of governance in this country to make every 
effort that this solemn commitment, this solemn legal obligation is honoured in 
letter and spirit.
